what_it_does: Many engineering and verification problems can be written as formulas that mix discrete choices (like true/false flags or integer decisions) with continuous quantities (like real-valued voltages or probabilities) — this combination is handled by tools called SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) solvers. Sometimes engineers do not just want to know whether such a formula has a solution; they want to count how many solutions exist, which reveals how likely a bug is or how large a design's safe operating region is. Counting solutions in hybrid discrete-continuous formulas is extremely hard, partly because earlier approaches that convert everything to pure binary logic (bit-blasting) cannot represent continuous variables at all. pact is an approximate counting method for these hybrid formulas: it uses random hash functions to partition the solution space into roughly equal-sized buckets, then counts solutions in one bucket and multiplies up — a hashing trick that is well-understood for purely discrete problems but here is extended to handle the continuous parts. It makes only a logarithmic number of calls to an underlying SMT solver (far fewer than brute-force enumeration) and provides mathematical guarantees on how far its count can be from the true answer.
